q:
A jury convicts Dorian Pratt of reckless homicide after a trial that turned on whether the victim could have seen Pratt's truck from a crosswalk 300 feet away. Two days later, juror Ellen Marsh tells defense counsel that during deliberations another juror pulled up a satellite image of the intersection on her phone, measured the sight line, and announced, "There's no way he couldn't see her." Marsh adds that the image "changed three votes, including mine." Pratt moves for a new trial and offers Marsh's affidavit.

Which part of the affidavit may the court consider?
o: None of it, because Rule 606(b) bars any juror testimony about anything that happened during deliberations.
All of it, because a juror's own research is an outside influence that Rule 606(b) does not reach at all.
Only her account that the image was brought into deliberations, not her account of its effect on any juror's vote.
All of it, because the Sixth Amendment overrides Rule 606(b) whenever a criminal jury was compromised.
Only her statement that it changed her own vote, because a juror may always describe her own reasoning.
e: Rule 606(b)(2)(A)–(C) allows juror testimony only about extraneous prejudicial information, outside influence, or a mistake on the verdict form. Even then, Rule 606(b)(1) bars testimony about the effect on any juror's vote or mental processes.
oe: Rule 606(b)(2)(A) is an exception for extraneous prejudicial information. A juror may testify that such information was brought to the jury's attention, even if that happened during deliberations.

The internet image is extraneous information under Rule 606(b)(2)(A), so testimony that it was brought in is allowed. But the exception doesn't open up the jurors' votes. Rule 606(b)(1) still bars testimony about the effect of anything on a juror's vote.

Correct. Rule 606(b)(2)(A) lets Marsh testify that extraneous prejudicial information was brought to the jury's attention. Rule 606(b)(1) still bars her testimony about the effect of anything on any juror's vote or mental processes. The court decides prejudice objectively, without asking jurors how they were swayed.
The only constitutional exception is Peña-Rodriguez, for clear racial bias relied on to convict. Tanner held that Rule 606(b) generally doesn't violate the Sixth Amendment.
A juror's own mental processes about the verdict are the core of what Rule 606(b)(1) bars.
topic: Jury Secrecy and Competency — Rule 606(b)(2)(A): what the juror may say

q:
Lionel Banks is charged with robbing a pharmacy on May 1. On May 22, two officers approached Banks outside his apartment to serve a bench warrant for unpaid child support. Banks knew about that warrant. He ran, and he was caught three blocks away. Nothing suggests he knew he was a suspect in the robbery. The prosecution offers the flight to show consciousness of guilt of the robbery, and Banks objects.

What is the court's best ruling?
o: Admit it, because flight from police always has some tendency to show consciousness of guilt.
Exclude it under Rule 404(b), because flight is a bad act offered to show the defendant's criminal character.
Admit it, because the weight of flight evidence is for the jury, and Rule 403 doesn't reach the accused's conduct.
Exclude it under Rule 403, because flight from an unrelated warrant says little about this robbery.
Exclude it as irrelevant, because flight three weeks after the crime can't make guilt any more probable.
e: Flight is relevant only through a chain of inferences: to flight, to consciousness of guilt, to guilt of the crime charged, and to actual guilt. When a link is weak, as when the defendant had another reason to flee, Rule 403 can exclude it.
oe: The evidence may clear Rule 401's low bar, but relevance isn't the end of the analysis. Rule 403 weighs how much it is worth.
Flight is offered for a chain of inferences about consciousness of guilt, not to show character. Rule 404(b) isn't the right objection.
Rule 403 applies to all relevant evidence, including the defendant's own conduct.

Correct. The Myers chain needs each link to hold: behavior to flight, flight to consciousness of guilt, guilt of the crime charged, and actual guilt. The third link fails when Banks had another reason to run. Explaining that reason would force him to reveal another wrong. Low probative value and real unfair prejudice let the court exclude it under Rule 403.
A three-week delay weakens the inference but doesn't eliminate it. Rule 401 requires only "any tendency."
topic: Relevance and Rule 403 — Flight: the Myers chain and Rule 403

q:
Rosa Kell is charged with murdering her business partner. She claims she stabbed him once in self-defense when he lunged at her. Before trial she offers to stipulate to the victim's identity and the cause of death. The prosecution refuses and offers three autopsy photographs. Together they show 14 stab wounds, six of them in the victim's back. Kell objects under Rule 403 and cites Old Chief.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude them, because Old Chief requires the prosecution to accept a defendant's stipulation to any element.
Exclude them, because autopsy photographs of a stabbing are inherently more prejudicial than probative.
Admit them, because their value on the disputed self-defense claim isn't substantially outweighed.
Admit them, because Rule 403 doesn't apply to evidence of facts the defense has offered to stipulate.
Admit them only if the prosecution shows that no less inflammatory proof of the wounds is available.
e: Under Rule 403, a concession lowers probative value only on the point conceded. Photos that bear on a disputed issue, such as self-defense, are admissible unless that value is substantially outweighed. Old Chief applies only to status elements.
oe: Old Chief is confined to proof of legal status, such as a prior-felony element. Ordinarily the prosecution may prove its case its own way.
Rule 403 has no per se rule against gruesome photos. In Bocharski, four of six photos came in because they bore on disputed issues.

Correct. The number and location of the wounds bear on the disputed claim of a single defensive blow. A stipulation to cause of death doesn't remove that probative value. Under Rule 403, exclusion requires that probative value be substantially outweighed. Bocharski excluded only photos with little value on any disputed issue.
Rule 403 applies to all relevant evidence. A concession reduces probative value on the 403 scale. It doesn't take the evidence outside the rule.
The availability of other proof is one factor in Rule 403 balancing. It isn't a threshold the prosecution must satisfy.
topic: Relevance and Rule 403 — Rule 403: stipulation outside Old Chief

q:
Hal Ortiz fell from a stepladder bought at Brightway Hardware and sued only the manufacturer, Apex Ladders, for failure to warn. A month after his fall, Brightway put its own stickers on every Apex ladder in stock: "Do not stand on top two steps." Apex had nothing to do with the stickers. Ortiz offers them to prove a warning was needed, and Apex objects under Rule 407.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude the stickers, because Rule 407 bars any post-accident measure offered to prove a need for a warning.
Admit the stickers, because Rule 407 doesn't apply in a products-liability case like this one.
Exclude the stickers, because they are relevant only if Apex itself adopted or approved them.
Admit the stickers, but only to impeach an Apex witness who says no warning was needed.
Rule 407 doesn't bar them, because Brightway isn't a party, though Rule 403 still applies.
e: Rule 407 bars a party's own post-injury measures offered to prove negligence, defect, or the need for a warning. Measures taken by nonparties fall outside its policy but remain subject to Rule 403.
oe: Rule 407's policy is to avoid discouraging a defendant from making repairs. A nonparty's measure doesn't implicate that policy, so courts generally don't apply the rule to it.
Since 1997, Rule 407 expressly covers product and design defects and the need for a warning. It does apply in products cases.
The stickers have some tendency to show a warning was needed, whoever posted them. Weakness goes to Rule 403, not to admissibility.
Impeachment is one permitted purpose, but it isn't the only route. Because Rule 407 doesn't apply to a nonparty's measure, the stickers may also be offered substantively.

Correct. Third-party remedial measures are generally admissible over a Rule 407 objection, because the rule's policy of encouraging defendants to make repairs isn't at stake. They are often weak, so Rule 403 may still exclude them.
topic: Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 407: remedial measures by a nonparty

q:
Corvin Foods sued Delta Freight for spoiled produce, claiming the shipment arrived on March 20, three weeks late. At a settlement meeting, Delta's operations chief said, "Our logs show the trucks reached your dock March 2. We'll offer $10,000 just to end this." At trial the same operations chief testifies that the trucks arrived "around March 18." Corvin offers testimony about the settlement-meeting remark to impeach him.

Is the remark admissible?
o: No, because Rule 408 bars negotiation statements offered to impeach by prior inconsistent statement.
Yes, because Rule 408 bars such evidence only when it is offered to prove liability, not to impeach.
Yes, because the remark is a statement of fact, and Rule 408 covers only offers of money.
Yes, because it is a statement of Delta's agent made within the scope of his employment.
Yes, under Rule 408(b), because it shows that the operations chief is biased in Delta's favor.
e: Rule 408(a) bars compromise offers and statements made in negotiations, on behalf of any party, to prove or disprove the validity or amount of a disputed claim or to impeach by inconsistency or contradiction. Rule 408(b) permits other purposes, such as bias.
oe: Correct. Rule 408(a) bars statements made during compromise negotiations offered to prove or disprove a disputed claim, "or to impeach by a prior inconsistent statement or a contradiction." The 2006 amendment closed the impeachment route.
This was the pre-2006 view in some courts. The text now expressly bars impeachment by inconsistency or contradiction.
Rule 408(a)(2) covers "conduct or a statement made during compromise negotiations," not just the offer itself.
Rule 801(d)(2)(D) only answers the hearsay objection. Rule 408 is a separate bar.
Proving that a witness changed his story is impeachment by inconsistency, not bias. Bias would be something like a settlement that gives a witness a stake in the outcome.
topic: Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 408: no impeachment by inconsistency

q:
Seconds after his car rear-ended Nia Grant's car, Owen Tate ran to her window and said, "I'm so sorry, I was reading a text. Don't worry, I'll pay your ambulance and hospital bills." Grant had not made any claim. In her negligence suit, she offers the whole statement through a bystander. Tate objects to all of it.

What is the proper ruling?
o: Exclude all of it under Rule 408, because it was an offer to resolve Grant's potential claim.
Exclude all of it under Rule 409, because statements made with an offer to pay are protected too.
Admit all of it, because Rule 409 covers only medical expenses actually paid, not promises to pay.
Admit his admission that he was reading a text, but exclude his offer to pay the bills.
Admit only the offer to pay, because an apology is inadmissible as an expression of sympathy.
e: Rule 409 excludes only the offer or payment of medical expenses to prove liability. Accompanying admissions remain admissible, which contrasts with Rule 408's protection of statements made in compromise negotiations.
oe: Rule 408 requires compromise of a claim disputed as to validity or amount. No claim existed yet, much less a dispute.
Unlike Rule 408, Rule 409 doesn't protect statements that accompany the offer. The ACN explains that such offers are made from humanitarian impulses, while statements of fact are not.
Rule 409 covers "furnishing, promising, or offering to pay" medical expenses, so the promise is protected.
Correct. Rule 409 excludes the offer to pay medical and hospital expenses to prove liability. It doesn't reach the factual admission, which comes in as Tate's own statement under Rule 801(d)(2)(A).
The Federal Rules have no apology exception, and Rule 409 is what bars the offer to pay. The slides contrast "Let me give you a bandaid" (barred) with "I'm so sorry" (admissible).
topic: Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 409: the offer goes, the admission stays

q:
Marco Bell is charged with assault. He claims the victim, Troy Quinn, swung first. In his case, Bell calls a witness who testifies that Quinn has a reputation in the neighborhood as a violent man. Bell doesn't testify. In rebuttal, the prosecution offers:

I. Testimony from Quinn's employer that, in her opinion, Quinn is a peaceful person.
II. Testimony from Bell's coworker that, in her opinion, Bell is a violent person.
III. Testimony from a bartender describing a fight Bell started at his bar last year.

Which items are admissible?
o: I only.
II only.
I and II only.
II and III only.
I, II, and III.
e: By attacking the victim's trait under Rule 404(a)(2)(B), the accused lets the prosecution rebut it and prove the accused's same trait. Under Rule 405(a), that proof must be reputation or opinion. Specific instances come in only on cross-examination.
oe: Item I is proper rebuttal under Rule 404(a)(2)(B)(i), but Item II is also admissible. When the defendant attacks the victim's trait, the prosecution may offer evidence of the defendant's same trait.
Item II is admissible, but so is Item I. The prosecution may rebut evidence of the victim's trait.

Correct. Once Bell offers Quinn's violent character, Rule 404(a)(2)(B) lets the prosecution rebut it (Item I) and offer evidence of Bell's same trait (Item II), even though Bell never offered his own character. Item III is a specific instance. Under Rule 405(a), character is proved by reputation or opinion, and specific acts come in only on cross of a character witness.
Item III fails Rule 405(a): extrinsic proof of a specific act is not a permitted way to prove character here. Item I is admissible.
Item III is barred by Rule 405(a). Character isn't an essential element of the charge or the defense, so Rule 405(b) doesn't apply.
topic: Character Evidence — Rule 404(a)(2)(B) opens the door; Rule 405(a) form

q:
At 9:00 p.m., Gil Moran argued with Victor Shaw at a bar, and Shaw insulted Moran's wife. Moran left, saying, "You'll be sorry." At 10:15 he bought a revolver at a pawnshop, and at 11:00 Shaw was shot dead outside the bar. Moran is charged with murder and claims he was home all night. The prosecution offers:

I. The pawnshop clerk's testimony about the 10:15 purchase.
II. Three rifles and a stun gun found in Moran's basement, none connected to the shooting.
III. A receipt showing Moran bought the stun gun two years earlier.

Which items are admissible over a character objection?
o: I only.
II only.
I and II only.
I and III only.
I, II, and III.
e: Under Rule 404(b)(2), another act is admissible only through a non-character chain of inference. Arming oneself right after a quarrel shows preparation. A general collection of weapons shows only character (People v. Zackowitz).
oe: Correct. A gun bought an hour after the quarrel and before the shooting shows preparation and opportunity, purposes Rule 404(b)(2) allows. Unconnected weapons, and the old receipt for one of them, show only that Moran is the "desperate type" who keeps an arsenal. That is the propensity inference People v. Zackowitz condemned.
The basement weapons are exactly what Cardozo held inadmissible in People v. Zackowitz: they prove only character.
Item II proves only a dangerous disposition.
Item III, an old stun-gun purchase, has no link to the shooting.
Items II and III have no non-propensity chain of inference.
topic: Character Evidence — Zackowitz: preparation vs. arsenal

q:
Wade Lyle is charged in federal court with molesting his nine-year-old niece. Seventeen days before trial, the prosecution disclosed a statement from Lyle's nephew, now 28, who would testify that Lyle molested him when he was eight. The nephew never reported it, and Lyle was never charged. Lyle objects that the act is uncharged, 20 years old, and offered only to show he is the kind of person who molests children.

What is the most likely ruling?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 414 admits only other acts of molestation that resulted in a conviction.
Admit it only for a Rule 404(b)(2) purpose such as plan or intent, with a limiting instruction.
Admit it without balancing, because Rule 414 makes other child molestation admissible as of right.
Exclude it unless the prosecution proves the earlier act by clear and convincing evidence.
Admit it, including for propensity, if a jury could find it occurred and Rule 403 allows.
e: Rules 413–415 let other sexual-assault or child-molestation acts be used for propensity. No conviction is needed, the Huddleston sufficiency standard applies, the proponent must disclose them 15 days before trial, and Rule 403 balancing applies as usual.
oe: Rules 413–415 require no conviction. Any other act of child molestation may qualify.
Rule 414(a) is a true exception to the propensity ban. The evidence "may be considered on any matter to which it is relevant," including propensity, so it needs no Rule 404(b) purpose.
Rule 414 says the court "may" admit. Rule 403 still applies with its normal balance (United States v. Guardia).
Courts use the Huddleston standard, under which a jury could reasonably find the act by a preponderance. Rule 414 has no clear-and-convincing requirement.

Correct. Rule 414(a) admits other acts of child molestation for any relevant purpose, including propensity. The act need only be provable under the Huddleston standard, and ordinary Rule 403 balancing still applies (Guardia). Remoteness counts in that balance but isn't a bar. Disclosure 17 days before trial met the 15-day requirement.
topic: Character Evidence — Rule 414: uncharged, decades-old act

q:
Harbor Mutual claims it mailed Lena Ruiz a policy cancellation notice on June 3, before her house burned. No employee remembers mailing that notice. Harbor's office manager testifies that for 11 years every cancellation notice has been printed, logged, stamped, and placed in a tray. A postal carrier collects the tray daily. The log shows a notice to Ruiz on June 3. Ruiz objects that the testimony is improper character evidence and is uncorroborated.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 404(a) bars an organization's character offered to prove conduct on one occasion.
Admit it to prove the notice was mailed, as evidence of an organization's routine practice.
Exclude it, because Rule 406 requires an eyewitness or other corroboration that the practice was followed.
Admit the log under Rule 803(6), but exclude the manager's description of the mailing practice.
Exclude it, because only individuals have habits; organizations act through individual decisions.
e: Rule 406 admits a person's habit or an organization's routine practice to prove action in conformity on a particular occasion. No corroboration or eyewitness is needed. The practice must be regular, specific, and semi-automatic.
oe: A routine practice isn't character. Rule 406 specifically admits it to prove conduct on a particular occasion.

Correct. Rule 406 admits evidence of an organization's routine practice to prove that it acted accordingly on a particular occasion, "regardless of whether it is corroborated or whether there was an eyewitness." A regular, specific mailing procedure is the classic example.
Rule 406 expressly dispenses with corroboration and eyewitnesses.
The log may be a business record, but the manager's testimony about the practice is independently admissible under Rule 406.
Rule 406 expressly covers "an organization's routine practice."
topic: Character Evidence — Rule 406: an organization's routine practice

q:
Andre Fisk is charged in federal court with burglary of a dwelling. His defense is that he was at a friend's apartment, and he is the only witness who can say so. If Fisk testifies, the prosecution wants to impeach him with his six-year-old state felony conviction for residential burglary. That conviction's elements required breaking and entering with intent to commit theft. No other impeachment of Fisk is available.

What is the most likely ruling?
o: Admit it, because every felony conviction must be admitted to impeach a testifying witness.
Admit it, because burglary with intent to steal is a crime of dishonesty under Rule 609(a)(2).
Exclude it, because its probative value doesn't outweigh its prejudicial effect to Fisk.
Admit it unless Fisk shows that its prejudice substantially outweighs its probative value.
Exclude it, because only crimes of dishonesty may be used against a testifying defendant.
e: Rule 609(a)(1)(B) admits a testifying defendant's felony only if its probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect to the defendant. Similarity to the charge and the importance of the defendant's testimony weigh against admission (the Gordon factors, applied in Brewer).
oe: Under Rule 609(a)(1)(B), a testifying criminal defendant's felony comes in only if the court finds that its probative value outweighs the prejudice to that defendant.
Theft and burglary are generally not crimen falsi. Proving their elements doesn't require a dishonest act or false statement.

Correct. Rule 609(a)(1)(B) uses a balance that favors the defendant, and the proponent bears the burden. Under the Gordon factors applied in United States v. Brewer, a prior identical to the charge invites propensity reasoning. A defendant whose testimony is central should not be deterred from giving it. Both factors weigh against admission, so the conviction is likely excluded.
That is the ordinary Rule 403 test, which applies to witnesses other than the accused under Rule 609(a)(1)(A). It isn't the standard for the defendant.
Felonies may impeach a defendant under Rule 609(a)(1)(B) if they pass its balancing test.
topic: Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Rule 609(a)(1)(B): same-crime prior; the Gordon factors

q:
In a civil fraud suit, the defendant wants to impeach the plaintiff's key witness with her conviction, 12 years ago, for filing a false insurance claim. The offense was a state misdemeanor, and she was fined and never confined. Its elements required proof of a knowingly false statement. The defendant gave written notice two months before trial.

What standard governs admission of the conviction?
o: It must be admitted with no balancing, because its elements required proof of a false statement.
It is inadmissible, because a misdemeanor can never be used to impeach a witness's truthfulness.
It is inadmissible, because Rule 609 bars all convictions that are more than 10 years old.
It is admitted unless its probative value is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice.
It comes in only if its probative value, shown by specific facts, substantially outweighs its prejudicial effect.
e: Rule 609(b) applies to any conviction more than 10 years past the later of conviction or release, including crimen falsi. It is a reverse 403 test: probative value must substantially outweigh prejudice, and the proponent must give written notice.
oe: Rule 609(a)(2) has no balancing, but Rule 609(b) overrides it for old convictions. The time limit applies to crimen falsi too.
Under Rule 609(a)(2), any crime whose elements required a dishonest act or false statement qualifies, whatever the punishment.
Rule 609(b) isn't an absolute bar. It raises the bar and requires notice.
That is Rule 403's standard. It governs recent felonies for non-defendant witnesses, not convictions more than 10 years old.

Correct. More than 10 years have passed since the conviction, and there was no confinement to restart the clock. Rule 609(b) applies even to crimen falsi. It admits the conviction only if probative value, supported by specific facts and circumstances, substantially outweighs prejudicial effect, and the proponent gave reasonable written notice.
topic: Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Rule 609(b): old crimen falsi

q:
In a bank-fraud trial, the defense attacks the character for truthfulness of the government's cooperating witness, Ivy Stone. The government then calls Stone's pastor, who testifies that in his opinion Stone is a truthful person. On cross, defense counsel asks the pastor, "Did you know that last year Ivy Stone lied about her income on a mortgage application?" The pastor says he did not. The defense then calls the loan officer to testify that the application was false.

Which ruling is correct?
o: The question is improper, because specific instances may be raised only with the witness herself.
The question is proper, and so is the loan officer's testimony, because the pastor opened the door.
The question is improper, because Stone's truthfulness can't be supported until she is convicted.
The question is proper, but the loan officer's testimony is barred extrinsic evidence.
Both are improper, because a mortgage application has nothing to do with a person's truthfulness.
e: Under Rule 608(b), the court may allow cross-examination about specific instances probative of truthfulness. That includes those of a witness whose character the cross-examined witness has vouched for. Extrinsic evidence of those instances is barred.
oe: Rule 608(b)(2) expressly allows inquiry into specific instances of another witness's conduct when cross-examining a witness who has testified about that witness's character for truthfulness.
Rule 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence of specific instances offered to attack or support character for truthfulness, no matter who opened the door. The examiner takes the answer.
Rule 608(a) permits rehabilitation once character for truthfulness has been attacked, and the defense attacked it.

Correct. The question is allowed under Rule 608(b)(2): it tests the basis of the pastor's opinion, and lying on a loan application is probative of untruthfulness. Rule 608(b) bars extrinsic proof of the act, so the defense must accept the pastor's answer.
A false statement on a financial application is a lie, which is the core of what bears on character for truthfulness.
topic: Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Rule 608(b)(2): cross of a character witness; no extrinsic proof

q:
Kara Dunn sues her former employer for sexual harassment by her supervisor. The employer moves, 20 days before trial, to offer coworkers' testimony that Dunn often told sexually explicit jokes at work and described her sex life at office parties. The employer argues this shows the supervisor's advances were not unwelcome.

What standard governs admission?
o: It is inadmissible, because Rule 412 permits only reputation evidence about a victim in civil cases.
It is admissible unless unfair prejudice substantially outweighs its probative value under Rule 403.
It is admissible only if its value substantially outweighs harm to Dunn and unfair prejudice.
It is inadmissible, because it fits none of the three exceptions listed in Rule 412(b)(1).
It is admissible, because Rule 412 applies only in criminal proceedings for sexual offenses.
e: In civil cases, Rule 412(b)(2) admits a victim's other sexual behavior or predisposition only if its probative value substantially outweighs the harm to the victim and unfair prejudice to any party. Reputation is admissible only if the victim placed it in controversy, and Rule 412(c) procedures apply.
oe: In a civil case, specific instances may come in under the Rule 412(b)(2) balancing test. Reputation is the more restricted form: it comes in only if the victim has placed it in controversy.
That is Rule 403's balance, which favors admission. Rule 412(b)(2) reverses it and places the burden on the proponent.

Correct. Rule 412(b)(2) admits evidence of a victim's sexual behavior or predisposition in a civil case only if its probative value substantially outweighs the danger of harm to any victim and of unfair prejudice to any party. The employer filed the motion more than 14 days before trial, as Rule 412(c) requires, and the court holds a sealed hearing.
Rule 412(b)(1) lists the exceptions for criminal cases. Civil cases use the balancing test in Rule 412(b)(2).
Rule 412(a) applies "in a civil or criminal proceeding involving alleged sexual misconduct."
topic: Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Rule 412(b)(2): civil reverse balancing

q:
Grant Hale died after falling from a hotel balcony. His life-insurance policy excludes suicide. His widow sues the insurer, which claims he jumped. The widow offers Hale's email to a friend, sent the night before he died: "Just booked our Alaska cruise for June. Can't wait to show Mia the glaciers!" She offers it to prove that Hale didn't intend to kill himself. The insurer objects that it is hearsay.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because no exception admits a statement offered to prove what the declarant would later do.
Admit it as a present sense impression, because Hale described the booking right after making it.
Admit it, because an implied assertion is never hearsay under the Federal Rules of Evidence.
Exclude it, because a dead declarant's statements come in only as dying declarations under Rule 804.
Admit it under Rule 803(3) as a statement of Hale's then-existing plan and emotion.
e: A statement of the declarant's own plan, motive, or emotion is admissible under Rule 803(3) to prove that state of mind and, through it, the declarant's later conduct (Mutual Life Insurance). Statements of memory or belief offered to prove the fact remembered or believed are excluded.
oe: Under the Hillmon doctrine, Rule 803(3) admits a statement of the declarant's own intent or plan to prove that the declarant later acted on it.
The email is offered to show Hale's plans and outlook, not to describe an event he was perceiving. Rule 803(1) is a poor fit.

Under Rule 801(a), a statement exists whenever the declarant intended an assertion. Hale intentionally communicated his plans and eagerness, so offering them for the belief behind them is hearsay. The outline uses a "Planning my retirement home" example on this point.
A dying declaration under Rule 804(b)(2) is one route, but Rule 803(3) applies whether or not the declarant is available.

Correct. Hale's statement of his plan and eagerness is hearsay when offered to show he didn't intend suicide. Rule 803(3) admits statements of the declarant's then-existing intent, plan, and emotional state, and they may be used to show his later conduct conformed (Mutual Life Insurance).
topic: Definition of Hearsay — Implied assertion of a plan; Rule 803(3)

q:
Agnes Polk's will left nothing to her son Tom. Tom contests the will, claiming Agnes suffered from an insane delusion when she made it. The will's proponent offers testimony from Agnes's neighbor that, a month before signing the will, Agnes said, "Tom is a thief. He stole my mother's ring." The proponent concedes that Tom stole nothing. The statement is offered to show that Agnes had a reason for disinheriting Tom, believed or not.

How should the court treat the statement?
o: As hearsay with no exception, because Agnes is unavailable and her statement accuses Tom of a crime.
As admissible to show Agnes's feelings toward Tom, but not to prove that Tom stole anything.
As admissible to prove Tom stole the ring, because Rule 803(3) admits statements of belief.
As a statement against Agnes's interest, because disinheriting her own son was contrary to it.
As inadmissible character evidence, because it portrays Tom as a thief to explain the will.
e: The same words can be hearsay for one purpose and not for another. Offered for the declarant's feelings or reasons, they come in (not for truth, or under Rule 803(3)). Offered to prove the fact believed, they are barred. Rule 105 instructs the jury on the limited use.
oe: Offered to show what Agnes felt and believed, not the truth of the theft, the statement isn't hearsay, or else it falls within Rule 803(3) as a statement of her then-existing state of mind.

Correct. The proponent offers the words for Agnes's feelings toward Tom and her reason for the gift, not to prove a theft. That is either a non-truth use or a statement of then-existing state of mind under Rule 803(3). A Rule 105 limiting instruction keeps the jury from using it to prove Tom stole.
Rule 803(3) excludes "a statement of memory or belief to prove the fact remembered or believed" (except about the declarant's will). To prove Tom stole, the statement is hearsay with no exception.
The statement isn't against Agnes's pecuniary or penal interest, and Rule 804(b)(3) requires an objective reasonable-person test.
The statement isn't offered to show Tom acted in character on some occasion, so Rule 404 isn't triggered.
topic: Definition of Hearsay — Not for its truth: the testator's belief

q:
In a cocaine-conspiracy trial against Dale Ruiz, the government offers a recorded call. In it, Rick Vance, an admitted dealer, tells a person he thinks is a new buyer (actually an informant): "Don't worry about supply. My guy Dale runs the tire shop on Elm. He fronts me a kilo every week." Ruiz does run a tire shop on Elm. The government offers no other evidence connecting Ruiz to Vance or to drug trafficking.

How should the court rule on Ruiz's hearsay objection?
o: Overrule it, because under Bourjaily the court may consider the statement itself in finding participation.
Overrule it, because the jury decides whether a conspiracy existed, and a jury could believe the call.
Sustain it, because a statement to a government informant can never be in furtherance of a conspiracy.
Sustain it, because the statement by itself can't establish that Ruiz participated in a drug conspiracy with Vance.
Overrule it, because Ruiz need not be charged with conspiracy for the coconspirator rule to apply.
e: For Rule 801(d)(2)(E), the judge finds the conspiracy, the party's participation, and that the statement was "during and in furtherance" by a preponderance under Rule 104(a) (Bourjaily). The statement counts but can't carry that burden alone.
oe: Bourjaily lets the court consider the statement, but the 1997 amendment says it "does not by itself establish" the conspiracy or the defendant's participation. Some independent evidence is required.
Bourjaily holds that the foundation is a Rule 104(a) question for the judge, decided by a preponderance, not a Rule 104(b) question for the jury.
A statement to someone the speaker believes is a buyer can further the conspiracy, for example by reassuring a customer. The flaw here is the lack of independent evidence.

Correct. Under Rule 801(d)(2), the statement "does not by itself establish" the existence of the conspiracy or the party's participation in it. Ruiz's running a tire shop on Elm is only an identifying detail, not evidence that he joined a drug conspiracy. Without independent evidence, the judge can't find his participation by a preponderance.
That's true, since no conspiracy charge is needed, but it doesn't solve the missing independent evidence of participation.
topic: Opposing Party and Prior Statements — Rule 801(d)(2)(E): bootstrapping alone isn't enough

q:
In a robbery trial, eyewitness Paula Grey identifies Joel Marks as the robber. On cross, defense counsel suggests only that her memory is unreliable: the robbery happened two years ago, at dusk, and she wasn't wearing her glasses. Counsel doesn't suggest she has any motive to lie. The prosecution then offers Grey's written statement to police, made an hour after the robbery. It describes the robber exactly as she did in her testimony.

How may the jury use the statement?
o: Not at all, because a prior consistent statement may be used only to rebut a charge of fabrication.
Only to evaluate Grey's credibility, not as substantive proof of what the robber looked like.
Not at all, because it wasn't made before a motive to fabricate could have arisen.
As substantive evidence, but only if Grey made the statement under oath at a proceeding.
As substantive evidence, if it actually rebuts the attack on Grey's memory.
e: Rule 801(d)(1)(B)(i) admits consistent statements to rebut a charge of fabrication or improper motive, and only pre-motive statements qualify (Tome). Rule 801(d)(1)(B)(ii) admits them to rehabilitate against other attacks, such as faulty memory. Both are substantive.
oe: Since 2014, Rule 801(d)(1)(B)(ii) also covers statements offered to rehabilitate a witness attacked "on another ground," such as faulty memory.
A statement that qualifies under Rule 801(d)(1)(B) isn't hearsay and comes in substantively. The 2014 amendment eliminated the line between rehabilitation and substance.
Tome's pre-motive requirement governs a charge of fabrication under (B)(i). No motive to lie was charged here.
Prior consistent statements need not be sworn. Only the old version of Rule 801(d)(1)(A) required an oath.

Correct. Grey testifies and is subject to cross. Her consistent statement, made soon after the event, rehabilitates her against the attack on her memory. Rule 801(d)(1)(B)(ii) makes such a statement non-hearsay, usable for its truth.
topic: Opposing Party and Prior Statements — Rule 801(d)(1)(B)(ii): rehabilitation after a memory attack

q:
After a beating that left him unable to speak, Ray Choi was shown a six-photo array in the hospital. When the detective pointed to Kyle Dorn's photo and asked, "Is this the man?", Choi nodded firmly. At Dorn's trial, Choi testifies that he remembers nodding at a photo, but he no longer remembers his attacker's face or why he picked that photo. The prosecution calls the detective to describe the nod. Dorn objects on hearsay and Confrontation Clause grounds.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit it, because a nod is nonverbal conduct and so is never a statement under Rule 801(a).
Exclude it, because Choi's memory loss makes him unavailable for cross-examination about it.
Exclude it, because an identification to a detective is testimonial and Choi can't be cross-examined.
Admit it as a prior identification by a witness who testifies.
Admit it only as a recorded recollection, read to the jury but not received as an exhibit.
e: Rule 801(d)(1)(C) admits a testifying witness's earlier identification of a person, even if the witness now can't remember the basis (United States v. Owens). Conduct intended as an assertion is a statement under Rule 801(a).
oe: Nonverbal conduct is a statement if the person intended it as an assertion, and a nod answering "Is this the man?" is assertive.
In United States v. Owens, the Court held that a witness who testifies and answers questions is "subject to cross-examination" even if he can't remember the basis for the identification.

When the declarant testifies at trial and submits to cross, the Confrontation Clause is satisfied (California v. Green; Owens). It guarantees an opportunity for effective cross, not cross that succeeds.

Correct. The nod is a statement because Choi intended it as an assertion. Rule 801(d)(1)(C) excludes from hearsay a testifying declarant's prior identification of a person he perceived earlier. Under Owens, memory loss doesn't defeat "subject to cross-examination," and the Confrontation Clause is satisfied.
Rule 803(5) requires a record the witness made or adopted when fresh and vouches for. A nod isn't a record.
topic: Opposing Party and Prior Statements — Rule 801(d)(1)(C): nod, memory loss, and Owens

q:
In a civil suit arising from an intersection crash, a firefighter testifies that about 40 minutes after the collision she freed passenger Leah Moss from the wreck. Moss was trembling, sobbing, and bleeding from the scalp. When the firefighter asked, "What happened?", Moss cried, "The truck ran the red light. It never even slowed down!" Moss can't be located for trial.

Is the firefighter's testimony about Moss's words admissible?
o: Yes, as an excited utterance, because Moss was still under the stress of the crash.
Yes, as a present sense impression, because Moss described an event she herself had perceived.
No, because a statement made in answer to a question can't be an excited utterance.
No, because 40 minutes is too long for any of the spontaneous-statement exceptions.
Yes, but only if the plaintiff first shows Moss is unavailable under Rule 804(a).
e: A Rule 803(2) excited utterance must relate to a startling event and be made while the declarant is still under its stress. Delay and questioning count but aren't disqualifying. Rule 803(1) requires near-contemporaneity, not stress.
oe: Correct. Rule 803(2) asks whether the declarant was still under the stress of excitement the startling event caused. Trapped, bleeding, and sobbing, Moss was. Time lapse and a simple question are factors, not bars. In this civil case, the Confrontation Clause isn't in play.
Rule 803(1) requires a statement made while or immediately after the declarant perceived the event. Forty minutes is too long.
A neutral question like "What happened?" doesn't by itself destroy spontaneity. The test is whether stress still dominated.
Rule 803(2) has no fixed time limit. Its duration depends on how long the stress lasts.
Rule 803 exceptions apply "regardless of whether the declarant is available."
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 803(2): delay and questioning

q:
Ben Ochoa sues for injuries from a rear-end collision. His lawyer sends him to Dr. Lane, who will not treat him and was hired only to examine him and testify. Ochoa tells Dr. Lane: (1) "Since the crash I've had shooting pains down my left leg"; (2) "The other car slammed into me from behind"; and (3) "The other driver was obviously drunk." Dr. Lane is asked to repeat all three statements at trial.

Which statements are admissible under Rule 803(4)?
o: None, because the exception covers only statements made to a doctor consulted for treatment.
All three, because each one describes the cause of Ochoa's injuries in some way.
Statements (1) and (2), because symptoms and general cause are pertinent but fault is not.
Statement (1) only, because statements about cause are never pertinent to diagnosis.
None, but Dr. Lane may disclose them to the jury as the basis of her opinion.
e: Rule 803(4) admits statements reasonably pertinent to diagnosis or treatment, including a consultation solely for testifying. That covers history, symptoms, inception, and general cause, but not fault or identity.
oe: Rule 803(4) covers statements made for "medical diagnosis or treatment." The ACN extends it to a physician consulted only to testify, which rejects the older common-law limit.
The other driver's intoxication goes to fault, not to the cause of the injury. It isn't reasonably pertinent to diagnosis.

Correct. Rule 803(4) covers symptoms and their general cause if reasonably pertinent to diagnosis, and diagnosis for litigation counts. Being hit from behind bears on the mechanism of injury. Whether the other driver was drunk is fault, which is ordinarily not pertinent.
The rule expressly covers "their general cause."
Statements (1) and (2) are substantively admissible under Rule 803(4), so they don't need Rule 703's restrictive disclosure route.
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 803(4): litigation-only physician; fault not pertinent

q:
Seth Varga sues Dana Ruiz for injuries suffered when Varga's motorcycle collided with Ruiz's car. Ruiz claims Varga was drunk. Ruiz offers a hospital emergency-room record, authenticated by the records custodian, that reads: "Pt states he had 'six or seven beers' before riding." Varga objects that the record is double hearsay.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because Varga had no business duty to the hospital, so his words can't be in its record.
Exclude it, because how much Varga drank isn't pertinent to his medical diagnosis or treatment.
Admit it, because the record and Varga's own statement each fit a hearsay route.
Admit it, because a hospital record comes in whole once the custodian lays the foundation.
Exclude it, because Rule 805 bars hearsay within hearsay in a business record.
e: Under Rule 805, each layer of a multi-level statement needs its own route. A business record covers the recorder. An outsider's statement inside it needs a separate basis, such as Rule 801(d)(2) when offered against that person.
oe: That is the Johnson v. Lutz problem. It means Varga's statement needs its own route, not that it is excluded. Here it has one.
This might defeat Rule 803(4), but that exception isn't needed. Varga's statement is offered against him.

Correct. Rule 805 requires an exception for each layer. The nurse's entry is a record of regularly conducted activity under Rule 803(6). Varga's own words, offered by his opponent, are not hearsay under Rule 801(d)(2)(A).
Business-record status covers only the entrant's layer. Each statement within it needs its own exception (Rule 805).
Rule 805 admits hearsay within hearsay if each part conforms with an exception.
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 805: business record carrying a party's own statement

q:
At a preliminary hearing on a robbery charge against Nate Cole, eyewitness Gina Pratt testified for the prosecution that she saw Cole take the money. As a matter of strategy, Cole's lawyer chose not to cross-examine her. By trial, Pratt herself has been charged in an unrelated case. When called, she invokes her privilege against self-incrimination, and the court upholds it. The prosecution offers the transcript of her preliminary-hearing testimony.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because Cole never actually cross-examined Pratt at the preliminary hearing.
Exclude it, because a witness who invokes a privilege isn't unavailable under Rule 804(a).
Admit it under the hearsay rule, but exclude it under the Confrontation Clause as testimonial.
Admit it, because Pratt is unavailable and Cole had an opportunity and similar motive to cross.
Admit it, because testimony given at a preliminary hearing isn't testimonial under Crawford.
e: Rule 804(b)(1) and Crawford both turn on an opportunity to cross-examine, not on whether it was used. A privilege ruling makes the declarant unavailable under Rule 804(a)(1).
oe: Both Rule 804(b)(1) and Crawford ask whether the party had an opportunity to cross-examine. A strategic choice not to use the opportunity doesn't defeat it.
Rule 804(a)(1) defines a declarant as unavailable when the court rules that a privilege exempts her from testifying.
Crawford is satisfied where the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. Both conditions are met.

Correct. Pratt is unavailable under Rule 804(a)(1). Under Rule 804(b)(1), her former testimony is admissible against Cole, who had an opportunity and a similar motive to develop it at the hearing on the same charge. The testimony is testimonial, but Crawford is satisfied by her unavailability and Cole's prior opportunity to cross.
Prior testimony at a preliminary hearing is at the core of what Crawford calls testimonial.
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 804(b)(1) and Crawford: an opportunity not used

q:
Police arrest Eddie Hart with stolen jewelry. In a recorded stationhouse interview after Miranda warnings, Hart says: "Yeah, I carried the bag out. But Lou Pike planned the whole thing, picked the house, and kept most of the take." At Lou Pike's federal trial for the burglary, Hart invokes the Fifth Amendment. The prosecution offers Hart's whole statement against Pike.

What is the correct ruling?
o: All of it is admissible, because the whole confession was against Hart's own penal interest.
The parts about Pike are admissible, because they were corroborated by the stolen jewelry.
The parts about Pike fail Rule 804(b)(3), and the Confrontation Clause bars them anyway.
All of it is admissible against Pike as a statement of his coconspirator in the burglary.
It is admissible only if Pike gets a chance to cross-examine Hart at this trial.
e: Rule 804(b)(3) admits only the specific remarks that are self-inculpatory (Williamson). Custodial statements to police are testimonial, so against a defendant they need unavailability plus a prior opportunity to cross (Crawford).
oe: Williamson holds that Rule 804(b)(3) admits only the individual remarks that are self-inculpatory, not the collateral parts of a broader confession.
Blame-shifting statements to police get "special suspicion" (Williamson), and corroboration doesn't make them testimonially safe.

Correct. Under Williamson, only remarks that are themselves against Hart's interest qualify, and naming Pike as the planner who took most of the take shifts blame. Independently, a Mirandized stationhouse statement is testimonial. Hart is unavailable and Pike never had a chance to cross-examine him, so Crawford bars it.
A confession to police after arrest isn't "during and in furtherance" of a conspiracy.
Hart invoked the privilege and didn't testify, so Pike had no opportunity to cross-examine.
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Williamson and Crawford: a blame-shifting confession

q:
Ana Ruiz and Ben Holt are tried together for a kickback scheme. The government offers an email Holt sent during the scheme to Cal Reyes, another participant: "Ana and I split the payment as soon as the invoices clear—keep the paperwork clean." Holt doesn't testify. Ruiz moves to exclude the email or sever her trial, citing Bruton.

How should the court rule?
o: Grant severance, because Bruton bars any nontestifying codefendant's statement naming the defendant.
Admit it against Holt only, with an instruction that the jury may not consider it against Ruiz.
Admit it only if Ruiz's name is replaced with a neutral phrase such as "my partner."
Admit it against both, because a nontestimonial coconspirator statement raises no Bruton issue.
Exclude it unless Holt takes the stand and submits to cross-examination about the email.
e: Bruton bars a nontestifying codefendant's facially incriminating confession that is inadmissible against the defendant. After Crawford, the statement must also be testimonial. A nontestimonial coconspirator statement admissible against both defendants raises no Bruton issue.
oe: Bruton applies only to statements inadmissible against the defendant, and after Crawford only to testimonial ones. This email is admissible against Ruiz.
No limiting instruction is needed, because the email is admissible against both defendants.
Redaction cures Bruton problems, but there's no problem to cure.

Correct. An email sent during and in furtherance of the scheme is admissible against Ruiz under Rule 801(d)(2)(E), and statements to a coconspirator are nontestimonial. Bruton reaches only statements inadmissible against the defendant, and the Confrontation Clause reaches only testimonial ones. The Problem 8.8 letter is the classroom example.
The Confrontation Clause doesn't apply to nontestimonial statements (Whorton), so Holt need not testify.
topic: Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Bruton: a nontestimonial coconspirator statement

q:
In a state murder trial, Floyd Kerr's defense is that Lyle Bates did the shooting. On the night of the killing, Bates separately told three close friends that he shot the victim. A fourth witness saw Bates holding a revolver of the type used minutes after the shots. Kerr calls Bates, who denies the killing. The state's voucher rule bars Kerr from cross-examining his own witness. The state's hearsay law has no exception for statements against penal interest, so the three friends are excluded. Kerr is convicted.

What is Kerr's strongest constitutional argument on appeal?
o: A Confrontation Clause violation, because Bates's out-of-court confessions were testimonial.
Due process: together, the rulings excluded critical, trustworthy defense evidence.
There is none, because states have complete authority to set their own rules of evidence.
A violation of Rule 804(b)(3), which binds state courts through the Fourteenth Amendment.
There is none, because Bates testified, so the jury heard his own account of the night.
e: Under Chambers, evidence rules may not be applied mechanistically to exclude critical, reliable defense evidence. Holmes adds that arbitrary or disproportionate exclusions violate the right to present a complete defense.
oe: The Confrontation Clause protects the defendant against the prosecution's evidence. Kerr's complaint is that his own evidence was excluded, which is a due-process and compulsory-process claim.

Correct. Chambers held that a voucher rule combined with a hearsay rule lacking a penal-interest exception denied due process. The excluded confessions were spontaneous, made to close friends soon after the crime, corroborated, and against interest, and the declarant was available for cross. Under Chambers, "the hearsay rule may not be applied mechanistically to defeat the ends of justice."
States have broad latitude, but the Constitution guarantees "a meaningful opportunity to present a complete defense" (Holmes).
The Federal Rules govern federal courts and don't bind a state trial. Rule 804(b)(3) also requires unavailability, and Bates testified.
Hearing Bates's denial while being barred from confronting him with his confessions is precisely the problem.
topic: Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Chambers: critical, trustworthy defense evidence

q:
Rita Vance calls 911 and screams, "He's hitting me—my husband, Carl Vance!" The dispatcher asks whether he has a weapon. Rita says, "No, his fists. He just ran out the back door." The dispatcher then asks a series of questions, and Rita, now calm, answers: Carl had been drinking since noon, he hit her twice last month, and he once broke her wrist. Rita refuses to testify at Carl's assault trial, and the prosecution offers the whole recording.

Which parts are admissible over Carl's Confrontation Clause objection?
o: All of it, because an emergency call is made to get help and so can never be testimonial.
None of it, because Rita's statements accuse Carl and she won't submit to cross-examination.
Only what she said during the attack and about the weapon, not her calm account of past abuse.
All of it, because a victim's statements about her own attacker are nontestimonial.
None of it, because Rita's refusal to testify forfeits the prosecution's use of her statements.
e: Statements to police are nontestimonial when their primary purpose is to meet an ongoing emergency, and testimonial once the purpose becomes establishing past events (Davis v. Washington). A conversation can shift from one to the other.
oe: Davis v. Washington held that a 911 call can become testimonial once the emergency ends and the questions turn to proving past events.
Statements whose primary purpose is to meet an ongoing emergency are nontestimonial and fall outside the Clause.

Correct. Under Davis v. Washington, Rita's statements during the attack and about the weapon were made to meet an ongoing emergency, so they are nontestimonial. Once Carl fled on foot, unarmed, and Rita calmly recounted past abuse, the primary purpose shifted to establishing past events. That made those statements testimonial, as in Hammon. Unlike in Michigan v. Bryant, no armed assailant posed a continuing threat to the public.
The victim's status doesn't decide the issue. In Hammon, the victim's statements were testimonial.
Forfeiture applies to a defendant who wrongfully procures the witness's absence (Giles), not to a witness's own refusal.
topic: Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Davis and Hammon: when a 911 call becomes testimonial

q:
In a dram-shop suit, the bartender who served Glen Ash testifies: (1) "When he left at 11, he was drunk. He was slurring, stumbling, and smelled strongly of beer." (2) "Based on the eight pints I poured him in two hours, his blood-alcohol level had to be at least .15." The bartender has no training in toxicology.

Which testimony is admissible?
o: Both, because the bartender personally perceived how much Ash drank and how he acted.
Neither, because intoxication is a medical conclusion that requires a qualified expert.
Only (2), because it rests on specific facts rather than on general impressions.
Only (1), because estimating blood-alcohol content requires specialized knowledge.
Both, because opinions on an ultimate issue are expressly allowed by Rule 704(a).
e: Rule 701 lay opinions must be rationally based on perception, helpful, and not based on specialized knowledge. Rule 701(c) keeps an expert in lay clothing from evading Rule 702 and its disclosure rules.
oe: Perception is necessary but not sufficient. Rule 701(c) bars a lay opinion based on specialized knowledge.
Intoxication with a foundation of observed signs is a classic lay opinion under the 2000 ACN.
Converting drinks to a blood-alcohol figure requires pharmacology, the kind of knowledge Rule 701(c) reserves to experts.

Correct. An opinion that someone was drunk, based on observed signs, is rationally based on perception and helpful (Rule 701(a)–(b)). A blood-alcohol estimate depends on scientific or specialized knowledge, which Rule 701(c) excludes from lay opinion. That opinion requires a qualified expert under Rule 702.
Rule 704(a) removes the ultimate-issue objection, but it doesn't make a lay witness competent to give a specialized opinion.
topic: Lay and Expert Opinion — Rule 701: lay opinion vs. specialized knowledge

q:
In a truck-collision case, the plaintiff's accident reconstructionist uses a momentum analysis that is widely accepted in the field. On voir dire he admits that he guessed the truck's weight at 18,000 pounds. The truck's registration shows 31,000 pounds, and his speed estimate changes substantially if the true weight is used. The defense moves to exclude. The plaintiff argues that the error goes to weight, not admissibility.

What should the court do?
o: Admit it, because once the method is generally accepted, errors in the inputs go only to weight.
Admit it, because Daubert tells courts to focus solely on methodology, not on conclusions.
Exclude it, because accident reconstruction is not a science, so it can't meet Daubert.
Admit it, because the credibility of an expert witness is always a question for the jury.
Exclude it unless the plaintiff shows, more likely than not, that it rests on sufficient data and a reliable application.
e: Under Rule 702 as amended in 2023, the court must find each requirement by a preponderance (Rule 104(a)), including sufficient facts or data and a reliable application of the method. Only attacks that remain after that finding go to weight.
oe: The 2023 ACN calls decisions treating sufficiency of basis and application as weight questions "an incorrect application of Rules 702 and 104(a)."
General Electric Co. v. Joiner held that "conclusions and methodology are not entirely distinct." An opinion separated from the data by too great an analytical gap may be excluded.
Kumho Tire holds that gatekeeping applies to all expert testimony. That means reliability screening, not automatic exclusion.
Rule 702 makes reliability a Rule 104(a) question for the court before the jury hears the opinion.

Correct. Since 2023, the proponent must show the court by a preponderance that the testimony is based on sufficient facts or data (702(b)) and that the opinion reflects a reliable application of the method to the facts (702(d)). A guessed input that contradicts the record and drives the result fails both. That is not merely a question of weight.
topic: Lay and Expert Opinion — Rule 702(b) and (d) as amended in 2023

q:
Sasha Lin received an anonymous phone call demanding $20,000 and threatening her family. She didn't recognize the voice. Six months later, while preparing for trial, a detective played Lin a recorded police interview of the defendant, Pete Varn. Lin immediately recognized the voice as the caller's. At trial the prosecution offers Lin's identification to authenticate the call as Varn's. Varn objects.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because familiarity with a voice acquired for litigation can't authenticate it.
Exclude it, because identifying a voice requires a qualified expert in voice analysis.
Admit it only if the judge finds by a preponderance that the caller was Varn.
Admit it, because she heard Varn's voice under circumstances connecting it to him.
Exclude it, because the call wasn't recorded, so the best evidence rule bars testimony about it.
e: Rule 901(b)(5) allows voice identification by anyone who has heard the voice at any time under connecting circumstances. Rule 901(b)(2) handwriting familiarity, by contrast, may not be acquired for the litigation. Authentication requires only evidence sufficient to support a finding.
oe: That limit applies to a nonexpert's handwriting opinion under Rule 901(b)(2). Rule 901(b)(5) has no such limit for voices.
Rule 901(b)(5) permits a lay opinion identifying a voice.
Authentication is a Rule 104(b) question. The judge asks only whether a reasonable jury could find the caller was Varn.

Correct. Rule 901(b)(5) allows identification of a voice "based on hearing the voice at any time under circumstances that connect it with the alleged speaker," even if the familiarity was acquired for trial. That is enough to support a finding. Varn can attack its reliability before the jury.
The best evidence rule applies only to proof of the content of a writing, recording, or photograph. Lin is testifying to what she heard, and no recording exists.
topic: Authentication and Best Evidence — Rule 901(b)(5): voice familiarity acquired for trial

q:
Maya Lowe met with attorney Carl Day about a dispute with her business partner. Early in the meeting she told him that two months earlier she had moved $60,000 of company funds into her personal account "to protect it." At the end of the meeting, Day said he couldn't take the case because of a conflict. A federal grand jury investigating embezzlement subpoenas Day to testify about what Lowe told him.

Must Day disclose the statement?
o: No, because a prospective client's confidences are privileged even when declined.
Yes, because no lawyer-client relationship was ever formed between Lowe and Day.
Yes, because the crime-fraud exception applies to a client's statements about a crime.
Yes, because the privilege protects communications, not underlying facts such as the transfer.
No, because the privilege belongs to the lawyer, so Day may simply decline to testify.
e: The lawyer-client privilege protects confidential communications made to obtain professional legal services, including those of a prospective client whose case is declined. It protects communications, not underlying facts, and the client holds it.
oe: Correct. The privilege covers prospective clients consulting a lawyer in a professional capacity, even if the lawyer later declines. Unlike in People v. Gionis, the lawyer hadn't made clear before the statement that he wouldn't act. Lowe was seeking legal help in confidence.
Prospective clients are covered. The question is whether Lowe consulted Day in his professional capacity, and she did.
The crime-fraud exception reaches advice sought to further a future or ongoing crime or fraud. A disclosure of past conduct while seeking advice is protected.

That's true but doesn't help the government here. The transfer itself can be proved by other means, and Lowe can't refuse to state it if asked. But Day can't be compelled to reveal what Lowe told him.
The privilege belongs to the client. Day asserts it on Lowe's behalf.
topic: Privileges — Lawyer-client: prospective client vs. Gionis

q:
Jon Reed is charged with a March bank robbery. In February, while they were dating, Reed privately told Wendy Cole, "I'm going to hit the bank on Main next month." In March, Cole saw Reed counting stacks of banded cash. They married in April, and the marriage is valid. At the federal trial in October, the prosecution calls Cole, who doesn't want to testify.

Which statement is correct?
o: Reed may prevent Cole from testifying, because the defendant-spouse holds the privilege.
Cole may refuse, but if she testifies, Reed can't block the statement or what she saw.
Cole must testify, because the privilege doesn't cover a marriage entered into after the crime.
Cole may refuse to testify about the February statement, but must testify to what she saw.
Reed may bar the February statement as a marital confidence, but Cole must testify to the cash.
e: Trammel: the witness-spouse holds the testimonial privilege, which requires a valid marriage when claimed and covers all adverse testimony in a criminal case against the spouse. The confidences privilege covers only confidential communications made during the marriage.
oe: Trammel modified Hawkins. The witness-spouse alone holds the testimonial privilege.

Correct. Under Trammel, the privilege against adverse spousal testimony belongs to the witness-spouse and requires a valid marriage when it is claimed, so Cole may refuse. If she testifies, Reed can't stop her. The marital-confidences privilege covers only communications made during the marriage, and the February statement was made before.
The federal testimonial privilege looks to a valid marriage when it is claimed, not when the crime occurred.
The testimonial privilege covers all adverse testimony, including acts observed. It isn't limited to communications.
The February statement was made before the marriage, so it isn't a marital confidence. And the witness-spouse may refuse all adverse testimony.
topic: Privileges — Spousal privileges: marriage after the crime

q:
In a federal civil-rights suit alleging that Officer Dana Price used excessive force, the plaintiff subpoenas the notes of a licensed clinical social worker who counseled Price in 40 sessions after the incident. The plaintiff argues that the notes are the only contemporaneous record of Price's account, and that the need for them outweighs any confidentiality interest. Price claims privilege.

How should the court rule?
o: Order production, because the privilege covers only psychiatrists and psychologists.
Order production, because the plaintiff's need for unique evidence outweighs Price's privacy.
Review the notes in camera and release the parts whose value outweighs the harm to Price.
Uphold the privilege, which covers licensed clinical social workers and isn't balanced away.
Order production, because Rule 501 makes federal courts apply state privilege law in civil cases.
e: Jaffee recognized a federal psychotherapist-patient privilege under Rule 501, covering licensed clinical social workers, with no case-by-case balancing. In civil cases, state privilege law applies only to state-law claims.
oe: Jaffee extended the privilege to licensed clinical social workers.
Jaffee rejected balancing: "An uncertain privilege ... is little better than no privilege at all."
This is a balancing approach in another form, which Jaffee rejected.

Correct. Under Rule 501's "reason and experience," Jaffee recognized a psychotherapist-patient privilege that covers licensed clinical social workers. It rejected ad hoc balancing of the evidentiary need against the patient's privacy.
State privilege law governs only claims for which state law supplies the rule of decision. A federal civil-rights claim is governed by federal common law.
topic: Privileges — Jaffee: social worker, no balancing

q:
After a federal jury returns a defense verdict in Luis Ortega's breach-of-contract suit, a juror signs an affidavit. It says the foreperson told the other jurors during deliberations, "You can't trust anything a Mexican says on the stand, and Ortega's whole case is his own word." Ortega moves for a new trial, relying on the affidavit.

May the court consider the affidavit?
o: Yes, because a juror's racial bias is extraneous prejudicial information under Rule 606(b)(2)(A).
Yes, because racial animus that motivated the verdict always overrides Rule 606(b).
No, because the constitutional exception for racial bias protects only criminal defendants.
Yes, because a juror's statement of bias is an outside influence improperly brought to bear.
No, because jurors may testify about racial bias only if the biased juror lied in voir dire.
e: Rule 606(b) bars juror testimony about deliberations except for extraneous information, outside influence, or a form error. The Peña-Rodriguez exception for clear racial animus is constitutional and applies only to criminal convictions.
oe: A juror's own beliefs and biases are internal matters, not extraneous information (Warger; Tanner).
Peña-Rodriguez rests on the Sixth Amendment right to an impartial jury in criminal cases. The outline lists three requirements: clear racial bias, a criminal case, and reliance on it to convict.

Correct. Rule 606(b)(1) bars juror testimony about statements made during deliberations. Peña-Rodriguez's exception rests on the Sixth Amendment and requires a criminal defendant convicted with clear racial animus as a significant motivating factor. A civil litigant can't invoke it.
An outside influence is pressure from outside the jury, such as a bribe or a threat. A juror's own prejudice isn't one.
Even a voir-dire challenge must be proved without testimony about deliberations (Warger). In any event, the exception doesn't depend on voir dire.
topic: Jury Secrecy and Competency — Peña-Rodriguez: civil cases

q:
Jill Park sues Ventra Corp. after her Ventra space heater ignited. To show that Ventra had notice of the defect before her injury, she offers a letter that another customer wrote to Ventra a year earlier describing an identical fire. The customer testifies that he addressed, stamped, and mailed the letter to Ventra's headquarters and that it was never returned. Ventra's mailroom supervisor testifies that the company has no record of receiving it.

How should the court decide whether the letter is admissible?
o: The court must find that Ventra more likely than not received the letter before admitting it.
The court should admit it if a reasonable jury could find receipt.
The court should exclude the letter as hearsay, because it describes an earlier fire.
The court should exclude it, because receipt is disputed and only Ventra's admission would do.
The court should admit it only if Park first proves the customer's account of the fire was true.
e: When relevance depends on a fact, such as receipt or knowledge, Rule 104(b) requires only evidence sufficient for a reasonable jury to find it, and the jury decides. Rule 104(a) questions, by contrast, are decided by the judge by a preponderance.
oe: Receipt is a fact on which relevance depends, so it is a Rule 104(b) question for the jury. The judge doesn't weigh the conflicting testimony (Huddleston).

Correct. The letter is relevant to notice only if Ventra received it. Under Rule 104(b), the judge asks only whether evidence could support a finding, and proper mailing could. The jury resolves the conflict with the mailroom testimony.
Offered to show that Ventra was told of a fire, the letter is not offered for its truth. Notice is a non-hearsay use.
Rule 104(b) requires only evidence sufficient to support a finding. A dispute doesn't defeat admission.
For notice, it doesn't matter whether the fire happened as described, only that Ventra was told about it.
topic: Relevance and Rule 403 — Rule 104(b): receipt as a conditional fact

q:
No eyewitness saw the face of a hit-and-run driver. Witnesses said the vehicle was a red pickup with a dog in the cab and a ponytailed male driver. The defendant owns a red pickup and a dog and wears a ponytail. The prosecution calls a statistics professor. Using estimates the prosecutor supplied, with no supporting studies (1 in 20 pickups are red, 1 in 8 have a dog, 1 in 10 drivers have a ponytail), the professor multiplies them. She testifies that the chance a random truck shares all three traits is 1 in 1,600. The defense objects.

What is the most likely ruling?
o: Admit it, because probability evidence is admissible whenever an expert does the math correctly.
Admit it, because the defense can expose any weakness in the numbers on cross-examination.
Exclude it, because probability evidence is never admissible to prove a person's identity.
Admit it, with an instruction that the jury may give the figure whatever weight it deserves.
Exclude it, because the numbers were assumed and the traits weren't shown to be independent.
e: Under Collins, probability evidence needs real data and independent factors. Assumed numbers multiplied together lack a foundation and invite overvaluation, which is unfair prejudice under Rule 403.
oe: Correct arithmetic on invented inputs produces a precise-sounding number with no basis.
People v. Collins reasoned that an impressive expert figure the defense can't refute is exactly what distracts a jury. Cross-examination doesn't cure a number with no foundation.
Probability evidence built on real data, such as DNA population frequencies, is admissible.
An instruction doesn't supply the missing foundation.

Correct. Collins reversed because the probabilities were simply assumed and the factors weren't independent (a ponytail and a dog in a pickup may well correlate). The figure also risked overwhelming the jury. Even an accurate figure wouldn't show that this defendant was the driver.
topic: Relevance and Rule 403 — Collins: assumed probabilities

q:
During plea negotiations with an Assistant U.S. Attorney, Mark Dale said, "I knew the brake parts failed testing when I sold them." The negotiations produced a guilty plea to wire fraud, which the court accepted. Dale was sentenced and didn't appeal. A trucking company that bought the parts now sues Dale for fraud and offers his statement from the plea negotiations.

Is the statement admissible?
o: No, because Rule 410 bars plea-discussion statements made to a prosecutor in any later case.
No, because Rule 408 bars statements made while negotiating to resolve a disputed claim.
Yes, because Rule 410 doesn't protect plea talks that ended in a guilty plea that still stands.
No, because only the judgment of conviction, not the statements behind it, may be used later.
Yes, but only to impeach Dale if he testifies that he didn't know about the test failures.
e: Rule 410 bars, against the defendant, withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, and statements in plea proceedings or in plea discussions with a prosecutor that didn't end in a guilty plea or ended in one later withdrawn. A plea that stands isn't protected.
oe: Rule 410(a)(4) is limited to discussions that "did not result in a guilty plea or ... resulted in a later-withdrawn guilty plea."
Plea bargaining is governed by Rule 410, and Rule 408(a)(2)'s criminal-case clause concerns regulatory claims. Neither protects these statements.

Correct. Rule 410(a)(4) protects statements in plea discussions with a prosecutor only if they didn't result in a guilty plea or resulted in a plea later withdrawn. Dale's plea stands, so the rule's policy of protecting failed negotiations doesn't apply. The statement comes in against him under Rule 801(d)(2)(A).
Nothing in Rule 410 limits a later case to the judgment.
Because Rule 410 doesn't apply at all, the statement is admissible substantively, not merely to impeach.
topic: Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 410: plea talks that ended in a guilty plea

q:
In January 2026, after internal testing, Halo Heaters redesigned the tip-over switch on its space heaters. Ken Ward had bought an older unit in 2024. In March 2026 it tipped over without shutting off and burned him. Ward sues Halo for a design defect and offers evidence of the January redesign. Halo objects under Rule 407.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because the redesign came after Ward's heater was manufactured and sold.
Rule 407 doesn't bar it, because the redesign came before Ward's injury, though Rule 403 still applies.
Exclude it, because Rule 407 applies to strict-liability design-defect claims.
Admit it only to prove feasibility, and only if Halo disputes feasibility.
Exclude it, because Rule 407 bars any design change offered to prove a defect.
e: Rule 407 bars only measures taken after the injury or harm in suit. Pre-injury changes fall outside it (subject to Rule 403). For measures within the rule, the "if disputed" purposes (ownership, control, feasibility) and impeachment remain.
oe: Rule 407 measures timing from the injury or harm sued on, not from manufacture or sale.

Correct. Rule 407 covers measures taken after the injury that would have made it less likely. A change made before Ward's injury falls outside the rule, as in the Wolf Attack timing example. Its admissibility turns on Rules 401–403.
That's true, but irrelevant. The rule doesn't reach measures taken before the injury.
The "if disputed" purposes are what the rule permits for a measure it otherwise bars. A pre-injury measure needs no such purpose.
Only measures taken after the injury are barred.
topic: Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 407: a change made before the injury

q:
Ella Brandt was hurt when a rotten board gave way on a boat dock behind Gary Lund's lake house. Lund denies that he owns or controls the dock, which he says belongs to his neighbor. Brandt offers Lund's homeowner's liability policy, which lists "dock and boat lift" as insured premises. Lund objects under Rule 411.

What is the proper ruling?
o: Exclude it, because evidence of liability insurance is inadmissible for any purpose.
Admit it to prove that Lund carelessly failed to maintain the dock he insured.
Exclude it unless Lund first opens the door by testifying that he has no insurance.
Admit it to prove ownership or control, with an instruction against inferring negligence.
Exclude it, because insurance evidence is admissible only to show a witness's bias.
e: Rule 411 bars insurance evidence only to prove negligence or wrongful conduct. It may be admitted for another purpose, such as bias, agency, ownership, or control, subject to Rule 403 and a limiting instruction.
oe: Rule 411 bars only one purpose: proving negligence or wrongful conduct.
That is the barred purpose.
Rule 411 has no such prerequisite. Ownership and control are independent permitted purposes.

Correct. Rule 411 permits insurance evidence for "another purpose," including "agency, ownership, or control." Lund disputes control, and insuring the dock tends to show it. A Rule 105 instruction limits the jury's use.
Bias is one example. Rule 411 also lists agency, ownership, and control.
topic: Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 411: insurance to prove control

q:
Paul Mariner, a company CEO, is on trial for bribery. Before indictment, prosecutors offered him immunity in exchange for information about other executives' payments. He replied that he knew of no payments by anyone, and the offer was withdrawn. At trial, the government proved consciousness of guilt by showing that Mariner moved large sums into gold after colleagues began cooperating. Mariner offers evidence of his rejection of immunity. The government objects that it is irrelevant and is plea-negotiation material.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 410 bars any evidence of plea or immunity discussions.
Exclude it, because declining an offer has no tendency to show innocence.
Admit it only if Mariner testifies and is subject to cross-examination.
Exclude it, because his own rejection of the offer is self-serving hearsay.
Admit it, because rejecting immunity tends to show consciousness of innocence.
