Later, in rebuttal, the plaintiff calls Kerr's neighbor, who would testify that the day after the crash Kerr told him, "The light had already turned yellow, but I figured I could make it." Kerr objects that he was never given a chance to explain or deny the statement.

How should the court rule?
o: Sustain it, because since 2024 the witness must get a chance to explain or deny first.
Overrule it, but admit the statement only to impeach Kerr, not as proof.
Overrule it, because the foundation rule doesn't apply to an opposing party's statement.
Sustain it, because the light's color is a collateral matter on rebuttal.
Overrule it, because the judge may always order otherwise under Rule 613(b).
e: Rule 613(b) requires an opportunity to explain or deny before extrinsic proof of a witness's inconsistent statement, ordinarily first since 2024. It doesn't apply to an opposing party's statement under Rule 801(d)(2), which is also substantive.
oe: Rule 613(b) expressly says it "does not apply to an opposing party's statement as defined in Rule 801(d)(2)."
As Kerr's own statement offered against him, it is admissible substantively under Rule 801(d)(2)(A).

Correct. Rule 613(b)'s foundation requirement excludes opposing parties' statements. Kerr's statement is admissible under Rule 801(d)(2)(A) to prove that the light was yellow, as well as to impeach him.
The color of the light is a central fact, not a collateral one.
The court's discretion exists ("unless the court orders otherwise"), but it isn't needed here because Rule 613(b) doesn't apply at all.
topic: Opposing Party and Prior Statements — Rule 613(b) doesn't apply to party statements

q:
In a civil suit arising from a hit-and-run that injured a cyclist, the plaintiff calls a police officer. He testifies that within a minute of the crash an unidentified woman ran up to him, breathless and pointing down the street. She shouted, "That blue van ran the light, hit the cyclist, and took off that way!" The woman left before giving her name. The defendant, who owns a blue van, objects.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because an unidentified declarant's statement can never be an excited utterance.
Admit it even with no sign she saw the crash, since Rule 602 covers only witnesses.
Exclude it unless the plaintiff first shows the woman is unavailable to testify.
Admit it only if the woman's identity is established before the end of trial.
Admit it as an excited utterance, if the circumstances show she likely saw the crash.
e: Spontaneous-statement exceptions (Rules 803(1) and (2)) require that the declarant perceived the event. That may be inferred from the circumstances and the statement itself, so an unidentified declarant's statement can qualify.
oe: Anonymity makes it harder to show that she perceived the event, but it doesn't bar the statement.
The ACN applies personal knowledge to hearsay declarants. The exception is justified only if she perceived what she described.
Rule 803 exceptions apply regardless of availability.
Identity isn't required. The question is whether she perceived the event and spoke under its stress.

Correct. Under Rule 803(2), a startling event and a statement made under its stress qualify. The declarant must have perceived the event. Timing, her breathless pointing, and the detail of her statement can show that she did. An unidentified bystander's statement may qualify (it could also be a Rule 803(1) present sense impression).
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Spontaneous statements: the declarant's personal knowledge

q:
In a civil battery suit brought on behalf of a four-year-old against her stepfather, the plaintiff calls the emergency-room doctor. She testifies that the child's mother brought the child in and said, "Her left arm has been swollen and she's cried every time it's touched since Tuesday. It happened when her stepfather yanked her up by that arm." The doctor's records don't reflect any discussion of the child's safety at home, and no one has testified about how the stepfather's identity bore on treatment.

Which part of the mother's statement is admissible under Rule 803(4)?
o: None, because Rule 803(4) covers only statements made by the patient herself.
All of it, because an abuser's identity is always pertinent to a child's treatment.
All of it, because the doctor actually relied on it in treating the child's arm.
None, because the mother had an obvious motive to blame the stepfather.
All but the stepfather's identity, absent a foundation that it bore on treatment.
e: Rule 803(4) covers statements, including by a parent for a child, describing history, symptoms, inception, and general cause, if reasonably pertinent to diagnosis or treatment. Fault and identity require a showing of pertinence (State v. Smith).
oe: Rule 803(4) isn't limited to the patient. The ACN covers statements by a family member seeking care for the patient.
Some courts admit the identity of a household abuser, but the proponent must show how identity affected treatment, and this record has no such foundation (State v. Smith).
Reliance doesn't extend the exception to statements not reasonably pertinent to diagnosis or treatment.
A motive to fabricate is a 403 or weight argument. It doesn't defeat a statement that fits the exception.

Correct. The symptoms, when they began, and the general cause (being yanked by the arm) are pertinent to diagnosing an arm injury. Who did it is ordinarily not pertinent. Without testimony that identity mattered to treatment, such as safety planning, it doesn't qualify (State v. Smith).
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 803(4): statements by a parent; identity of the abuser

q:
In a civil suit over a highway collision, the plaintiff offers the investigating officer's report. The officer has since died. The report contains (1) the officer's measurements of 90 feet of skid marks behind the defendant's SUV, and (2) a line reading: "Witness (bystander, name unknown) stated the SUV was going 'at least 80.'" The defendant objects to the report.

What is the proper ruling?
o: Admit (1), but exclude (2) unless the bystander's statement fits its own exception.
Admit the whole report, because everything in a police report is a public record.
Exclude the whole report, because police reports are inadmissible in any case.
Admit (2) only, as the bystander's present sense impression recorded by the officer.
Exclude the whole report, because the dead officer can't be cross-examined.
e: Rule 803(8) covers what the officer observed and recorded under a duty (in civil cases, or against the government in criminal cases). Statements by outsiders inside the record need their own exception under Rule 805 (Johnson v. Lutz).
oe: Correct. Matters the officer observed under a legal duty to report are admissible under Rule 803(8)(A)(ii) in a civil case. The bystander had no duty to report, so his statement is a second layer that needs its own exception under Rule 805 (Johnson v. Lutz). Nothing shows when he spoke or under what stress.
The public-records exception covers the officer's layer, not statements of outsiders recorded in the report.
The criminal-case limit in Rule 803(8)(A)(ii) doesn't apply in civil cases.
Nothing shows that the bystander spoke while or immediately after perceiving the event.
The Confrontation Clause doesn't apply in civil cases, and Rule 803 exceptions don't depend on availability.
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 803(8) plus Rule 805: a bystander inside a police report

q:
Leo Marsh is on trial in federal court for fraud. He offers testimony that his former business partner, Rafael Cruz, told a friend, "I faked the invoices myself. Leo never knew." Cruz now lives in Brazil, beyond the reach of a subpoena. Marsh made no effort to arrange a deposition, though one could have been taken. The prosecution argues that Cruz isn't unavailable.

Is Cruz unavailable for purposes of the statement-against-interest exception?
o: Yes, because he lives abroad, beyond the reach of the court's subpoena power.
Yes, because any declarant who has moved out of the country is unavailable.
No, because Marsh also had to try to obtain Cruz's testimony, as by deposition.
It doesn't matter, because a statement against interest doesn't require unavailability.
Yes, because unavailability fails only when the proponent caused the declarant's absence.
e: Rule 804(a)(5) defines absence as unavailability only if the proponent couldn't procure attendance (for former testimony) or attendance or testimony (for dying declarations, statements against interest, and family history) by process or reasonable means.
oe: That would satisfy Rule 804(a)(5)(A) for former testimony, but for Rules 804(b)(2)–(4) the proponent must also seek the declarant's testimony.
Absence isn't enough. The proponent must show that reasonable means of obtaining attendance or testimony failed.

Correct. Under Rule 804(a)(5)(B), for exceptions (b)(2), (3), and (4), the proponent must show it couldn't procure the declarant's "attendance or testimony" by process or other reasonable means. Marsh didn't try to depose Cruz.
Rule 804(b)(3) is among the exceptions that require unavailability.
The proponent's wrongdoing is one way to fail Rule 804(a), but the proponent must also make the required showing.
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 804(a)(5)(B): try to get the testimony

q:
Wes Dunn, a member of a drug ring, testified before a federal grand jury against the ring's leader, Paul Kerr. A month before trial, another member, Cal Ruiz, told Kerr that Dunn "will be taken care of before he can testify." Kerr replied, "Do what you have to." Ruiz killed Dunn. At Kerr's trial, the government offers Dunn's grand jury testimony. The court finds these facts by a preponderance.

How should the court rule on Kerr's hearsay and Confrontation Clause objections?
o: Sustain both, because Kerr didn't personally cause Dunn's death or absence.
Sustain both, unless Kerr has first been convicted of murdering Dunn.
Overrule both, because Kerr forfeited them by acquiescing in the killing.
Overrule the hearsay objection, but sustain the confrontation objection.
Sustain both, because forfeiture must be proved by clear and convincing evidence.
e: Rule 804(b)(6): a party that wrongfully caused or acquiesced in causing a declarant's unavailability, intending that result, forfeits the hearsay objection. The same intent forfeits the confrontation right (Giles). Preponderance under Rule 104(a).
oe: Rule 804(b)(6) reaches a party that "wrongfully caused—or acquiesced in wrongfully causing" the unavailability.
No conviction is required. The judge decides the foundation under Rule 104(a).

Correct. Under Rule 804(b)(6), a party that acquiesced in wrongdoing intended to make the declarant unavailable forfeits the hearsay objection. The 1997 ACN uses a preponderance under Rule 104(a). Forfeiture by wrongdoing with that intent also defeats the confrontation right (Giles), even for testimonial statements.
Crawford and Giles recognize forfeiture as an exception to confrontation when the defendant intended to prevent testimony.
The ACN to Rule 804(b)(6) uses a preponderance standard.
topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 804(b)(6): acquiescence in wrongdoing

q:
Lena Cho testified before a grand jury, under oath, that she saw the defendant with a gun at the scene. At trial, she takes the stand and testifies that she never saw the defendant with a gun and that the police pressured her. She answers all questions on cross. The prosecution offers her grand jury testimony as substantive evidence, and the defense objects on hearsay and Confrontation Clause grounds.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit it, because Cho testifies subject to cross and the statement was sworn.
Exclude it, because grand jury testimony is testimonial and wasn't subject to cross.
Admit it only to impeach Cho, because she now recants the earlier account.
Exclude it unless the prosecution shows Cho is unavailable to testify.
Admit it only under the residual exception, after reasonable written notice.
e: A declarant who testifies and submits to cross at trial satisfies the Confrontation Clause for her prior statements (California v. Green). Inconsistent grand jury testimony is substantive under Rule 801(d)(1)(A).
oe: Correct. When the declarant testifies at trial and submits to cross, the Confrontation Clause places no limit on her prior statements (California v. Green; Crawford). Her sworn grand jury testimony, inconsistent with her trial testimony, is not hearsay under Rule 801(d)(1)(A), under either the old or the amended version.
Prior cross isn't needed when the declarant is cross-examined at trial (Green).
Rule 801(d)(1)(A) makes it substantive, and it was given under penalty of perjury at a proceeding.
Rule 801(d)(1) assumes the declarant testifies. Unavailability belongs to Rule 804.
Rule 807 applies only to statements not admissible under Rules 803 or 804. This statement isn't hearsay at all.
topic: Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Green: a declarant who testifies

q:
At a robbery trial, the prosecution plays part of Dean Wolfe's recorded police interview: "Yeah, I was at First Federal that afternoon." Two hours later in the same interview, Wolfe had said, "I didn't rob anybody. You've got the wrong guy." The defense asks the court to require that the denial be played immediately under Rule 106. The prosecution objects that it is self-serving hearsay.

What is the best ruling?
o: Play it now, because Rule 106 now overrides a hearsay objection to any other part.
Play it now, but only for context, with an instruction not to use it for its truth.
Decline, because the denial only contradicts the admission; it corrects no misimpression.
Play it now, because since 2023 Rule 106 applies to oral and recorded statements.
Decline, because Rule 106 never permits the introduction of hearsay statements.
e: Rule 106 (as amended in 2023) covers oral statements and overrides hearsay objections, but only for a remainder that in fairness ought to be considered to correct a misimpression. A general denial doesn't complete an admission (ACN, citing the Second Circuit).
oe: The amendment lets completion overcome a hearsay objection only when fairness requires it, because the remainder corrects a misimpression.
Completion comes in only if fairness requires it. There is no misimpression to put in context.

Correct. Rule 106 is narrow: the remainder must be needed to correct a misimpression. "I was at the bank" isn't made misleading by omitting a general denial of guilt hours later. The ACN, citing a 2019 Second Circuit decision, says a denial doesn't come in merely because it contradicts an admission.
Rule 106 does now cover oral statements, but the threshold of fairness still applies.
Since 2023, Rule 106 completion may be admitted "over a hearsay objection" when fairness requires it.
topic: Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Rule 106: a later denial doesn't complete an admission

q:
Two hours after a mugging, the victim, Joy Park, came to the police station. She was still shaking and crying. In a recorded interview, a detective asked her to describe the attack step by step, and she identified the mugger as her neighbor, Sam Ortiz. Park died in an unrelated accident before trial, and Ortiz never had a chance to cross-examine her. At Ortiz's trial, the prosecution offers the recording as an excited utterance.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit it, because a statement within a firmly rooted hearsay exception satisfies confrontation.
Exclude it, because it is testimonial and Ortiz never had a chance to cross Park.
Admit it, because Park's obvious stress makes the statement especially reliable.
Exclude it, because Park's death in an unrelated accident means she isn't unavailable.
Admit it, because the Confrontation Clause doesn't apply once the declarant is dead.
e: Evidence against a criminal defendant must satisfy both the hearsay rules and the Confrontation Clause. A testimonial statement of an absent declarant requires unavailability plus a prior opportunity to cross (Crawford), however reliable or excited the statement.
oe: That was the Ohio v. Roberts test, which Crawford overruled for testimonial statements.

Correct. Hearsay and confrontation are separate hurdles. A structured stationhouse interview about a completed crime, with no ongoing emergency, is testimonial (Crawford; Hammon). Testimonial statements require unavailability and a prior opportunity to cross. Death supplies the first but not the second.
Under Crawford, "Dispensing with confrontation because testimony is obviously reliable is akin to dispensing with jury trial because a defendant is obviously guilty."
Death makes a declarant unavailable whatever the cause, but unavailability alone isn't enough.
Death supplies unavailability, but Crawford also requires a prior opportunity to cross. Forfeiture would apply only if Ortiz caused her absence intending to prevent testimony (Giles).
topic: Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Crawford: an excited utterance can still be testimonial

q:
In a federal civil-rights suit alleging excessive force, the plaintiff's police-practices expert would testify: (1) "Officer Vance's use of a chokehold on a handcuffed, compliant man departed from nationally accepted police training standards"; and (2) "The force he used was unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment and constituted excessive force." The officer moves to exclude both.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit both, because Rule 704(a) permits opinions that embrace an ultimate issue.
Exclude both, because expert testimony on police practices isn't helpful to jurors.
Admit (2) only, because it addresses the exact question the jury must decide.
Admit (1), but exclude (2) because it states a legal conclusion about the force.
Exclude both, because police practices aren't a scientific field under Daubert.
e: Under Rule 704(a), an opinion embracing an ultimate issue is allowed, but experts may not state legal conclusions or tell the jury what result to reach (Hygh). In criminal cases, Rule 704(b) also bars opinions on the defendant's mental state.
oe: Rule 704(a) removes the ultimate-issue objection but doesn't admit opinions that instruct the jury on law or tell it what result to reach.
How officers are trained is specialized knowledge beyond common experience.
Statement (2) is the problem: it applies a legal standard and announces the verdict.

Correct. Testimony about professional standards helps the jury evaluate the conduct. Calling the force "unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment" and "excessive" states a legal conclusion that tells the jury how to decide. Hygh v. Jacobs held such testimony must be excluded.
Kumho Tire applies Rule 702 to "technical, or other specialized knowledge," not just science.
topic: Lay and Expert Opinion — Rule 704(a) vs. Hygh legal conclusions

q:
In a medical-malpractice trial, the plaintiff's expert, a neurologist, never examined the plaintiff. She was in the courtroom for the plaintiff's witnesses. She bases her opinion on (1) the plaintiff's hospital chart, already in evidence, and (2) a hypothetical question whose assumed facts the trial evidence supports. She then states her opinion that the delay in diagnosis caused permanent nerve damage. The defense objects that she has no personal knowledge and didn't first lay out every underlying fact.

How should the court rule?
o: Sustain it, because an expert must examine a patient before opining on her condition.
Sustain it, because the Federal Rules abolished the use of hypothetical questions.
Overrule it, but only if every fact she relied on is independently admissible.
Sustain it, because an expert must testify to the underlying facts before her opinion.
Overrule it, because experts need no personal knowledge and may give the opinion first.
e: Rule 703 bases: personal observation, facts made known at the hearing (including hypotheticals supported by the evidence), and facts experts reasonably rely on even if inadmissible. Rule 705 allows the opinion first, with bases disclosed on cross.
oe: Rule 703 lets experts base opinions on facts "made aware of," and Rule 602's personal-knowledge requirement expressly doesn't apply to expert opinion.
Hypothetical questions remain permissible under Rule 703. They are no longer required.
Rule 703 allows reliance on inadmissible facts of a kind experts in the field reasonably rely on.
Rule 705 lets an expert state an opinion and reasons without first testifying to the underlying facts, unless the court orders otherwise. They may be required on cross.

Correct. Rule 703's bases include facts made known at the hearing, by observing testimony or through a hypothetical supported by the evidence. Rule 602 doesn't apply to expert opinion. Under Rule 705, she may give the opinion first, and the defense can probe the bases on cross.
topic: Lay and Expert Opinion — Rule 703 bases: hypothetical questions; no personal knowledge

q:
In an arson-for-profit prosecution, the government calls a fire investigator with 25 years of experience. He would testify that "pour patterns" on the floor prove an accelerant was used. The defense moves for a Rule 702 hearing. It offers studies showing that such patterns often appear in accidental fires after flashover. The trial court denies the hearing, reasoning that the investigator's testimony rests on experience rather than science, so Daubert doesn't apply.

Was the ruling correct?
o: Yes, because Daubert's gatekeeping applies only to scientific testimony.
Yes, because 25 years of experience establishes reliability as a matter of law.
Yes, because challenges to an expert's method go to weight, not admissibility.
No, because the court must assess reliability of experience-based testimony too.
No, because fire investigation must be generally accepted under Frye before it is admitted.
e: Kumho Tire: Rule 702 gatekeeping covers all expert testimony. The court applies the Daubert factors that fit and has latitude in how to assess reliability, but it must assess it. Since 2023, the proponent proves each Rule 702 element by a preponderance.
oe: That was the Eleventh Circuit's view, which Kumho Tire reversed.
Experience can qualify a witness, but the court must still find that the method is reliable and reliably applied (Rule 702(c)–(d)).
Under Rule 702 as amended in 2023, reliability is a Rule 104(a) question for the court, decided by a preponderance.

Correct. Kumho Tire holds that the gatekeeping duty applies to "scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge." The court may use whichever Daubert factors fit, such as testing and error rates. It has discretion in how to test reliability, but not whether to. With studies showing that pour patterns appear in accidental fires, it must decide whether this method can reliably separate arson from accident.
Daubert held that Frye didn't survive the Federal Rules. General acceptance is one factor, not a requirement.
topic: Lay and Expert Opinion — Kumho Tire: experience-based testimony still gets gatekeeping

q:
A Coast Guard officer boarded Sal Rizzo's fishing boat 20 miles offshore and found 300 kilos of cocaine. At Rizzo's federal trial for importation, the officer testifies that the boat's GPS unit "showed that the boat had come from Mexican waters." The government offers no printout, photograph, or data from the GPS unit and gives no reason why it can't. Rizzo objects.

How should the court rule?
o: Overrule it, because the officer testifies from personal knowledge of what he saw.
Overrule it, because the best evidence rule applies only to writings, not electronic data.
Overrule it, because the GPS unit is an object, like a knife, and objects aren't covered.
Sustain it, because the testimony proves the content of a recording without the original.
Sustain it, because GPS evidence must be authenticated by a qualified expert witness.
e: Rule 1002 requires the original (or a duplicate under Rule 1003) to prove the content of a writing, recording, or photograph, including electronically stored data, unless Rules 1004–1007 excuse it. Testimony about an event that was also recorded is not proof of content.
oe: The officer didn't see the boat in Mexican waters. He is relaying what the device recorded, which is its content.
Rule 1001 defines writings and recordings to include electronically stored information, and an accurate printout of it is an "original."
The stored data is a recording. The device isn't being offered as an object. Its contents are being used as proof.

Correct. Under Rule 1002, proving the content of a recording requires an original or duplicate unless an exception applies. In the Bennett case, testimony about what a GPS device's stored data showed was proof of content. With no original and no Rule 1004 excuse, the testimony is inadmissible.
Authentication may be done by a witness with knowledge or by describing the process (Rule 901(b)(9)). The problem here is the best evidence rule.
topic: Authentication and Best Evidence — Best evidence: testimony about stored GPS data

q:
In a 2026 slip-and-fall case against Corner Mart, the plaintiff offers a 2022 local newspaper article. It reports that city inspectors cited the store for "standing water near the coolers on several occasions." She offers it to prove that the store had a recurring water problem. The paper's masthead and date appear on the clipping. The store objects.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit it, because a newspaper is self-authenticating under Rule 902(6).
Exclude it, because a newspaper must be authenticated by testimony from its publisher.
Admit it under the ancient-documents exception, as a dated news article.
Exclude it as hearsay, even though the article is self-authenticating.
Admit it as a public record of what the city inspectors found.
e: Under Rule 902, self-authenticating items need no extrinsic proof of genuineness, but they must still satisfy the hearsay rule and the best evidence rule. A modern newspaper offered for its truth is hearsay.
oe: Rule 902(6) satisfies authentication only. The article must still pass the hearsay rule.
Under Rule 902(6), printed material purporting to be a newspaper needs no extrinsic evidence of authenticity.
Rule 803(16) covers only documents prepared before January 1, 1998.

Correct. Rule 902(6) makes the article self-authenticating, but authentication is only the first gate. Offered to prove recurring water, it is the reporter's hearsay about what inspectors found, with another layer from the inspectors themselves. No exception covers the article.
The newspaper isn't a record of a public office. The city's own inspection records might qualify under Rule 803(8), but the reporter's account of them doesn't.
topic: Authentication and Best Evidence — Rule 902(6) self-authentication isn't a hearsay exception

q:
Federal prosecutors charge Ian Holt with tax evasion. His wife, Mira, is willing to testify against him, and they remain married. The prosecution wants her to testify that (1) one night at home Ian told her privately, "I'm hiding income in the Cayman account. Don't tell anyone," and (2) she saw him shredding bank statements in the garage. Mira had no part in the scheme. Ian claims privilege as to both.

What is the correct ruling?
o: Mira may testify to both, because under Trammel the witness-spouse alone decides.
Mira may testify to both, because communications about a crime aren't privileged.
Mira may testify to neither, because Ian holds the spousal testimonial privilege.
Ian may block (1) as a marital confidence, but Mira may testify to (2).
Ian may block (1), but only if he and Mira are divorced before trial.
e: Two spousal privileges: the testimonial privilege (the witness-spouse holds it, in criminal cases, during a valid marriage: Trammel) and the confidences privilege (either spouse, for confidential communications during the marriage, surviving divorce, with joint-crime and crimes-against-family exceptions: Rakes).
oe: Trammel governs the adverse-testimony privilege. The separate marital-confidences privilege lets either spouse prevent disclosure of a confidential marital communication.
The joint-crime exception requires the holder's complicity (United States v. Rakes). Mira wasn't a participant.
Under Trammel, the testimonial privilege belongs to the witness-spouse, and Mira waives it by choosing to testify.

Correct. The marital-confidences privilege covers confidential communications during a valid marriage, and either spouse may prevent disclosure. Because Mira wasn't complicit, the joint-crime exception doesn't apply (Rakes). Observations of conduct aren't communications. Mira holds and waives the testimonial privilege, so she may describe the shredding.
The confidences privilege survives divorce. It doesn't depend on it.
topic: Privileges — Marital confidences: Trammel doesn't let the spouse waive

q:
A federal grand jury investigating a warehouse fire subpoenas Diane Moore to testify about what her 17-year-old son told her in their kitchen the night after the fire. She believes he confessed to setting it. She moves to quash, arguing that compelling a parent to reveal a child's confidences would destroy family trust. She notes that her state's law recognizes a parent-child privilege.

How should the court rule?
o: Quash it, because Jaffee recognized privileges for relationships of trust and confidence.
Quash it, because the son was a minor when he confided in his mother.
Quash it, because federal courts must apply state privilege law under Rule 501.
Quash it, because the marital-confidences privilege extends to the whole family.
Deny the motion, because federal common law recognizes no parent-child privilege.
e: Under Rule 501, federal common law governs privilege in federal criminal proceedings. Without consensus in "reason and experience," courts decline to recognize new privileges such as parent-child, which contrasts with Jaffee.
oe: Jaffee rested on "reason and experience," including all 50 states' recognition. Courts have refused to extend it to parents and children for lack of that consensus.
The court in In re Grand Jury Proceedings rejected a privilege for minor children too.
State privilege law applies only in civil cases to claims governed by state law. A federal grand jury investigation is governed by federal common law.
The marital-confidences privilege protects spouses only.

Correct. In re Grand Jury Proceedings (3d Cir. 1997) held there is no parent-child privilege: almost every court rejects it, few states recognize it, it didn't exist at common law, and any such privilege should come from Congress. In this federal criminal proceeding, Rule 501 calls for federal common law.
topic: Privileges — No federal parent-child privilege

q:
In a federal age-discrimination suit, Norvane Corp. defends by claiming it relied in good faith on its lawyer's advice that the layoffs were lawful. To support that defense, Norvane intentionally produces one memo from outside counsel approving the layoff plan. The plaintiff then demands all of Norvane's other communications with counsel about the layoffs, including emails in which counsel raised concerns. Norvane says it waived privilege only for the one memo.

Which ruling is correct?
o: Waiver extends to other communications on the same subject that fairness requires.
Only the memo is disclosed, because Rule 502 limits waiver to the document produced.
All of Norvane's privileged communications on any subject at all are waived.
Nothing is waived, because the production was a reasonable litigation choice.
The waiver extends beyond the memo only if the disclosure was inadvertent.
e: Rule 502(a): an intentional waiver extends to undisclosed material only if it concerns the same subject and in fairness ought to be considered together. Inadvertent disclosures are governed by Rule 502(b).
oe: Correct. Under Rule 502(a), an intentional disclosure in a federal proceeding extends to undisclosed communications if they concern the same subject matter and in fairness ought to be considered together. A party can't use favorable advice as a sword while shielding contrary advice on the same layoffs.
Rule 502(a) limits subject-matter waiver to fairness situations, and this is the classic one.
Waiver doesn't reach unrelated subjects. Rule 502(a) is limited to the same subject matter.
An intentional disclosure is a waiver. The question is only its scope.
It is the opposite: an inadvertent disclosure never triggers subject-matter waiver under Rule 502(a), and may be no waiver at all under Rule 502(b).
topic: Privileges — Rule 502(a): subject-matter waiver
